snip.t: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Location: 60-70% occur in the HEAD of the pancreas.
snip.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review — Study Notes

qs.q: A 65-year-old man is diagnosed with invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Analysis of tumor tissue for molecular alterations reveals a point mutation most frequently found in over ninety percent of such malignancies. Which gene is this?
o: TP53 tumor suppressor
KRAS proto-oncogene
SMAD4 gene alteration
BRCA2 tumor suppressor
qs.e: Activating mutations in the KRAS gene are present in over 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas and drive early tumorigenesis. TP53 mutations are also common but occur at a lower frequency than KRAS.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which genetic alteration is present in the majority of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas and drives uncontrolled cell proliferation?
o: Germline BRCA2 mutation contributing to cancer susceptibility
Loss of SMAD4 tumor‑suppressor function in tumor cells
Inactivation of CDKN2A cell‑cycle regulator in pancreatic cancer
Activating KRAS mutation driving uncontrolled cellular proliferation
qs.e: KRAS is mutated in >90% of PDACs, leading to constitutive signaling. The other genes are also involved but occur less frequently.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: What is the most common location of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma within the pancreas?
o: Tumor situated in the body of the pancreas
Tumor located in the pancreatic tail region
Tumor arising in the pancreatic head area
Tumor originating from the uncinate process of the pancreas
qs.e: 60–70% of PDACs arise in the head, often causing biliary obstruction. The other sites are less common origins.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, which histologic feature contributes most to the tumor’s hard consistency and poor drug delivery?
o: Presence of necrotic cores within the tumor mass
Production of mucin by tumor cells contributing to gelatinous texture
High mitotic index indicating rapid tumor cell division
Dense desmoplastic stromal reaction surrounding cancer cells
qs.e: A dense desmoplastic stroma makes PDAC hard and hampers chemotherapy penetration. The other features are not responsible for firmness.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which risk factor is considered the strongest modifiable contributor to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
o: Consumption of a high‑fat diet as a risk factor
Family history of BRCA2 mutation as a genetic risk
Obesity contributing to increased pancreatic cancer risk
Smoking identified as the strongest modifiable risk factor
qs.e: Smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor for PDAC. The other factors are either non‑modifiable or less impactful.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which histologic feature is most indicative of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma on microscopic examination?
o: Well-formed, uniform glands with low N:C ratio
Irregular glands with desmoplastic stroma and high N:C ratio
Clusters of neuroendocrine cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin
Sheets of mucin-filled cysts lined by columnar epithelium
qs.e: PDAC shows irregular glands, high N:C ratio, and desmoplastic reaction. The other descriptions correspond to benign cysts or neuroendocrine tumors.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following best explains why pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma often presents with back pain?
o: Compression of the inferior vena cava
Perineural invasion by tumor cells
Metastasis to the lumbar vertebrae
Obstruction of the pancreatic duct causing pancreatitis
qs.e: Perineural invasion leads to referred back pain. While metastasis can cause pain, the primary mechanism is nerve involvement.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which genetic mutation is found in >90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cases?
o: BRCA2
SMAD4
KRAS
qs.e: Activating mutations in the KRAS oncogene are the most common genetic alteration in pancreatic cancer, present in nearly all cases.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour of the exocrine pancreas, most often in the head. It grows slowly, spreads early, and presents with vague abdominal pain and weight loss.

sections.p: PDAC is a malignant epithelial tumour arising from pancreatic ductal cells. Diagnosis requires imaging and histology. The tumour is usually hypovascular on CT and shows glandular structures on biopsy.

t.b: Tumour marker; elevated > 37 U/mL suggests PDAC but is not specific.
Provides tissue for cytology; confirms malignant ductal cells.
Defines tumour size, vascular involvement, and distant spread.

sections.p: The TNM system stages PDAC from I (localized) to IV (metastatic). Stage determines resectability and prognosis.
b: T: tumour size and local invasion

sections.p: Risk factors include smoking, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, obesity, and genetic syndromes. Environmental toxins and diet also contribute.
Patients report dull epigastric pain radiating to the back, early satiety, weight loss, and sometimes jaundice if the tumour blocks the bile duct.
Work‑up combines imaging, tumour markers, and tissue diagnosis. In low‑resource settings, ultrasound and CA 19‑9 can guide referral.

t.b: Detects mass or biliary dilatation; limited sensitivity but useful where CT unavailable.
Elevated levels support diagnosis; normal does not exclude PDAC.
Staging and surgical planning; if unavailable, MRI is alternative.
Histology confirms adenocarcinoma; essential before treatment.

sections.p: Rapid weight loss, obstructive jaundice, new‑onset diabetes, or haemorrhage from tumour invasion are urgent signs.

Treatment follows tumour stage. Resectable disease gets surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy; unresectable disease receives palliative chemo or radiotherapy. Supportive care addresses pain and nutrition.
b: Nutrition – high‑protein diet and pancreatic enzyme supplements

sections.p: Regular imaging and CA 19‑9 monitoring detect recurrence. Prevention focuses on smoking cessation, weight control, and managing chronic pancreatitis.
Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic pseudocyst, and neuroendocrine tumours can mimic PDAC clinically and on imaging.
b: Neuroendocrine tumour – usually hypervascular and hormonally active

sections.p: CA 19‑9 can be normal in early disease or elevated in benign biliary obstruction. Small tumours may be missed on ultrasound.
b: Ultrasound sensitivity – small head lesions may be invisible

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain, jaundice, unexplained weight loss, new‑onset diabetes, or haemorrhage

faq.q: Why is CA 19‑9 not a definitive test?
faq.a: It is sensitive but not specific; many benign conditions raise it, and some tumours do not produce it.
A low‑fat, high‑fiber diet and avoiding smoking reduce risk, but genetics also play a major role.

faq.q: What is the role of surgery?
faq.a: Surgery offers the only chance for cure in resectable disease, but most tumours are advanced by diagnosis.

exam: Explain the TNM staging of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on treatment options.
Describe the typical clinical presentation of a tumour in the head of the pancreas and why jaundice may occur.
Outline the first‑line chemotherapy regimen for unresectable PDAC and justify its use.
